newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian strike talks end in deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Colombian strike talks end in deadlock.

text.p: Marathon talks aimed at ending a nationwide strike by Colombia's public sector workers broke down early on Friday with no sign of an agreement soon, negotiators said.

Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, lead negotiator for the government, said the talks ended in a deadlock after 17 hours of heated bargaining at a building housing the national archives in downtown Bogota.
No date was set for a resumption of negotiations and the strike, which entered its fourth day on Friday, threatened to drag on indefinitely, he said.

Serpa said the main obstacle to a settlement was the insistence, by union leaders representing 800,000 state workers across the country, on a 21.5 percent pay hike to compensate for inflation of more than 21 percent last year.
The government, which is battling to cut its yawning fiscal deficit, has vowed to hold most public sector workers to a 13.5 percent increase.
"The salary issue weighs a lot," Serpa told the Caracol radio network. "Unfortunately, we weren't able to make any progress on the issue."

Luis Eduardo Garzon, head of the country's leading labour group, the Unitary Workers' Confederation, said the government had basically killed off any hope of a negotiated settlement by refusing to budge on the wage issue.
"We'll only return (to the bargaining table) if the government modifies its offer substantially," he said.

There have been conflicting reports on the impact of the strike, which led to mass protests in Bogota and other leading cities on Thursday when workers took to the streets to back demands for wage hikes and an end to planned privatisations.
Union officials say they have succeeded in disrupting key economic and social sectors, including oil, telecommunications, education and all but emergency health care.
But the government says only 10 percent of state workers have heeded the strike call and schools and universities are the only areas seriously affected by the work stoppage.

Despite threats from National Liberation Army rebels to provide "armed support" for the strike, and government warnings that leftist guerrillas were trying to infiltrate the strike movement, no serious violence has been reported since it began at midnight on Monday.
